claim: Trypanosomes have a trypanothione redox metabolism that provides reducing equivalents for numerous essential processes, most being mediated by tryparedoxin (Tpx).
source: Trypanosomes have a trypanothione redox metabolism that provides the reducing equivalents for numerous essential processes, most being mediated by tryparedoxin (Tpx).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to review articles (Krauth-Siegel and Leroux, 2012; Manta et al., 2018 and Manta et al., 2013) in the introduction.

claim: The biosynthesis and reduction of trypanothione are cytosolic.
source: While the biosynthesis and reduction of trypanothione are cytosolic, the molecular basis of the thiol redox homeostasis in the single mitochondrion of these parasites has remained largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction indicating that enzymes involved in T(SH)2 biosynthesis and TR appear to be restricted to the cytosol.

claim: The molecular basis of thiol redox homeostasis in the single mitochondrion of trypanosomes has remained largely unknown.
source: While the biosynthesis and reduction of trypanothione are cytosolic, the molecular basis of the thiol redox homeostasis in the single mitochondrion of these parasites has remained largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Tpx-roGFP2 is a superior probe for the trypanothione redox couple.
source: We show that the novel Tpx-roGFP2 is a superior probe for the trypanothione redox couple and that the mitochondrial matrix harbors a trypanothione system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing faster and stronger responses of Tpx-roGFP2 compared to other sensors.

claim: The mitochondrial matrix harbors a trypanothione system.
source: We show that the novel Tpx-roGFP2 is a superior probe for the trypanothione redox couple and that the mitochondrial matrix harbors a trypanothione system.
evidence: This is a major finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that mitochondrial sensors respond to trypanothione redox changes.

claim: Inhibition of trypanothione biosynthesis by Eflornithine impairs the ability of the cytosol and mitochondrion to cope with exogenous oxidative stresses.
source: Inhibition of trypanothione biosynthesis by the anti-trypanosomal drug Eflornithine impairs the ability of the cytosol and mitochondrion to cope with exogenous oxidative stresses, indicating a direct link between both thiol systems.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing delayed sensor recovery in DFMO-treated cells.

claim: There is a direct link between the cytosolic and mitochondrial thiol systems.
source: Inhibition of trypanothione biosynthesis by the anti-trypanosomal drug Eflornithine impairs the ability of the cytosol and mitochondrion to cope with exogenous oxidative stresses, indicating a direct link between both thiol systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibiting cytosolic trypanothione biosynthesis affects mitochondrial redox responses.

claim: Tpx depletion abolishes the cytosolic sensor response to H2O2.
source: Tpx depletion abolishes the cytosolic, but only partially affects the mitochondrial sensor response to H2O2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no sensor response in Tpx-depleted cells with cytosolic sensors.

claim: Tpx depletion only partially affects the mitochondrial sensor response to H2O2.
source: Tpx depletion abolishes the cytosolic, but only partially affects the mitochondrial sensor response to H2O2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing reduced but not abolished mitochondrial sensor response in Tpx-depleted cells.

claim: The mitochondrion harbors some Tpx and another, as yet unidentified, oxidoreductase.
source: This strongly suggests that the mitochondrion harbors some Tpx and, another, as yet unidentified, oxidoreductase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mitochondrial sensors still respond to H2O2 after Tpx depletion, though less efficiently.

claim: Trypanosomatids are the causative agents of African sleeping sickness, Nagana cattle disease, South-American Chagas' disease, and leishmaniasis.
source: Trypanosomatids are the causative agents of African sleeping sickness (Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense), Nagana cattle disease (Trypanosoma b. brucei, T. congolense), South-American Chagas' disease (T. cruzi) and the different manifestations of leishmaniasis (Leishmania spp.).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about trypanosomatid parasites.

claim: All trypanosomatid parasites lack glutathione reductases and thioredoxin reductases but have a trypanothione/trypanothione reductase system.
source: All these parasitic protozoa lack the nearly ubiquitous glutathione reductases (GRs) and thioredoxin reductases but, instead, have a trypanothione (T(SH)2)/trypanothione reductase (TR) system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the unique redox metabolism of trypanosomatids.

claim: The trypanothione system delivers reducing equivalents for a large number of vital processes.
source: The trypanothione system delivers reducing equivalents for a large number of vital processes (for reviews see Krauth-Siegel and Leroux, 2012; Manta et al., 2018 and Manta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Most reactions in the trypanothione system are mediated by tryparedoxin (Tpx), a distant member of the thioredoxin family.
source: Most of the reactions are mediated by tryparedoxin (Tpx), a distant member of the thioredoxin family.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the overall context of the manuscript.

claim: Trypanothione is synthesized from two molecules of glutathione linked by one molecule of spermidine, with glutathionylspermidine as intermediate.
source: For T(SH)2 synthesis, two molecules of glutathione (GSH) are linked by one molecule of spermidine, with glutathionylspermidine (Gsp) as intermediate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanothione biosynthesis, supported by citations (Comini et al., 2004; Krauth-Siegel and Leroux, 2012; Oza et al., 2002).

claim: Both steps of trypanothione synthesis are catalyzed by trypanothione synthetase (TryS).
source: Both steps are catalyzed by trypanothione synthetase (TryS) (Comini et al., 2004; Krauth-Siegel and Leroux, 2012; Oza et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: DFMO (Eflornithine) is a drug against late-stage T. b. gambiense sleeping sickness.
source: Difluoromethylornithine (DFMO, Eflornithine), a drug against late-stage T. b. gambiense sleeping sickness, is an irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), the enzyme generating putrescine, the precursor for spermidine synthesis.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about DFMO.

claim: DFMO is an irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC).
source: Difluoromethylornithine (DFMO, Eflornithine), a drug against late-stage T. b. gambiense sleeping sickness, is an irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), the enzyme generating putrescine, the precursor for spermidine synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of DFMO.

claim: Treatment of T. brucei with DFMO decreases the levels of spermidine and T(SH)2 and slightly increases the level of GSH.
source: Treatment of T. brucei with DFMO decreases the levels of spermidine and T(SH)2 and slightly increases the level of GSH (Bellofatto et al., 1987; Fairlamb et al., 1987; Xiao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: All enzymes involved in T(SH)2 biosynthesis and TR appear to be restricted to the cytosol.
source: All enzymes involved in T(SH)2 biosynthesis and also TR, which catalyses the NADPH-dependent reduction of trypanothione disulfide (TS2) as well as glutathionylspermidine disulfide (Gsp2), appear to be restricted to the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated based on existing knowledge about the localization of these enzymes.

claim: African trypanosomes lack catalase.
source: African trypanosomes lack catalase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the antioxidant systems of African trypanosomes.

claim: Hydroperoxides in African trypanosomes are detoxified by 2-Cys-peroxiredoxins (Prxs) and non-selenium glutathione peroxidase-type enzymes (Pxs).
source: Hydroperoxides are detoxified by 2-Cys-peroxiredoxins (Prxs) (Budde et al., 2003; Tetaud et al., 2001; Wilkinson et al., 2003) and non-selenium glutathione peroxidase-type enzymes (Pxs) (Hillebrand et al., 2003; Schlecker et al., 2005; Wilkinson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Pxs preferably reduce lipid hydroperoxides.
source: The Pxs preferably reduce lipid hydroperoxides (Bogacz and Krauth-Siegel, 2018; Diechtierow and Krauth-Siegel, 2011; Hiller et al., 2014; Schaffroth et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Prxs mainly detoxify hydrogen peroxide and peroxynitrite.
source: whereas the Prxs mainly detoxify hydrogen peroxide and peroxynitrite (Thomson et al., 2003; Trujillo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Both Pxs and Prxs are reduced by the TR/T(SH)2/Tpx system and act as tryparedoxin peroxidases.
source: Both types of thiol peroxidases are reduced by the TR/T(SH)2/Tpx system and thus act as tryparedoxin peroxidases (Scheme 1; Castro and Tomás, 2008; Krauth-Siegel and Comini, 2008; Krauth-Siegel and Leroux, 2012; Manta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Scheme 1.

claim: T. brucei encodes three virtually identical Pxs which occur in the cytosol (Px I and II) and the mitochondrion (Px III).
source: T. brucei encodes three virtually identical Pxs (Hillebrand et al., 2003) which occur in the cytosol (Px I and II) and the mitochondrion (Px III).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Depletion or deletion of the Pxs is lethal.
source: Depletion or deletion of the Pxs is lethal (Diechtierow and Krauth-Siegel, 2011; Hiller et al., 2014; Schaffroth et al., 2016; Schlecker et al., 2005; Wilkinson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Survival and proliferation of cells lacking Pxs can be restored by supplementing the medium with an iron chelator or Trolox.
source: However, survival and proliferation of cells lacking Pxs can be restored by supplementing the medium with an iron chelator or the vitamin E analogue Trolox [(±)−6-hydroxy-2,5,7,8-tetramethylchromane-2-carboxylic acid] (Bogacz and Krauth-Siegel, 2018; Diechtierow and Krauth-Siegel, 2011; Hiller et al., 2014; Schaffroth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Cell death of Px-deficient procyclic T. brucei closely resembles ferroptosis in mammalian cells.
source: Cell death of Px-deficient insect stage procyclic (PC) T. brucei closely resembles ferroptosis in mammalian cells (Bogacz and Krauth-Siegel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: T. brucei expresses two different Prxs, one in the cytosol (cPrx) and one in the mitochondrion (mPrx).
source: In the case of the Prxs, two different enzymes are expressed, one in the cytosol (cPrx) and one in the mitochondrion (mPrx) (Tomás and Castro, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In bloodstream T. brucei, depletion of cPrx, but not of mPrx, is lethal.
source: In bloodstream (BS) T. brucei, depletion of cPrx, but not of mPrx, is lethal (Wilkinson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In Leishmania, mPrx is required for survival of the parasite in the mammalian host, but this function is not related to its peroxidase activity but to its ability to act as a thiol-independent molecular chaperone.
source: In Leishmania, mPrx is required for survival of the parasite in the mammalian host. However, this essential function is not related to its peroxidase activity but to the ability of the protein to act as a thiol-independent molecular chaperone (Castro et al., 2011; Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The thiol-disulfide redox state of roGFP2 can be monitored in real time, inside intact cells, in a ratiometric manner.
source: The thiol-disulfide redox state of roGFP2 (reduction-oxidation-sensitive green fluorescence protein 2) can be monitored in real time, inside intact cells, in a ratiometric manner (Meyer et al., 2007; Meyer and Dick, 2010; Schwarzländer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on roGFP2.

claim: Equilibration of roGFP2 with the intracellular glutathione redox couple is mediated almost exclusively by glutaredoxins (Grxs).
source: Importantly, this approach allows to measure the degree of probe oxidation independently of absolute sensor concentration. Equilibration of the roGFP2 thiol-disulfide redox couple with the intracellular glutathione redox couple was found to be mediated, almost exclusively, by glutaredoxins (Grxs) (Meyer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Fusion of roGFP2 to human glutaredoxin 1 (hGrx1) generated a probe for specifically measuring the redox potential of the glutathione redox couple.
source: Thus, fusion of roGFP2 to human glutaredoxin 1 (hGrx1) generated a probe for specifically measuring the redox potential of the glutathione redox couple (EGSH) which is a function of both the GSH:GSSG ratio and total glutathione concentration (Gutscher et al., 2008; Morgan et al., 2013; Morgan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: hGrx1-roGFP2 has been used to measure changes in EGSH in various model organisms and compartments.
source: The hGrx1-roGFP2 fusion protein proved to be a valuable tool for measuring changes in EGSH in various model organisms and compartments (Gutscher et al., 2008; Kojer et al., 2012; Morgan et al., 2013; Radzinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: hGrx1-roGFP2 has been used to follow drug-induced changes of EGSH in Plasmodium falciparum and T. brucei.
source: It has also been used to follow drug-induced changes of EGSH in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum (Kasozi et al., 2013) and in T. brucei (Franco et al., 2017b; Franco et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Fusion of roGFP2 to mycoredoxin-1 yielded a probe selectively responding to changes in the mycothiol redox potential in actinomycetes.
source: For instance, fusion of roGFP2 to mycoredoxin-1 yielded a probe selectively responding to changes in the mycothiol redox potential in actinomycetes (Bhaskar et al., 2014; Reyes et al., 2018; Tung et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In yeast and human cells, GSH biosynthesis is confined to the cytosol.
source: In yeast and human cells, GSH biosynthesis is confined to the cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GSH biosynthesis in these organisms.

claim: GSH must be imported into both the intermembrane space (IMS) and the matrix of the mitochondrion.
source: GSH must therefore be imported into both the intermembrane space (IMS) and the matrix of the mitochondrion (Calabrese et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In yeast, the hGrx1-roGFP2 probe revealed that the cytosol, IMS and mitochondrial matrix rapidly recover after exposure of cells to an oxidant.
source: In yeast, the hGrx1-roGFP2 probe revealed that the cytosol, IMS and mitochondrial matrix rapidly recover after exposure of cells to an oxidant (Kojer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In yeast, GR localizes to both the cytosol and the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Indeed, GR localizes to both the cytosol and the mitochondrial matrix (Calabrese et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Trypanosomatids contain both free GSH and T(SH)2.
source: Trypanosomatids contain both free GSH and T(SH)2 (Ariyanayagam and Fairlamb, 2001; Krauth-Siegel and Comini, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Trypanosomes have a single mitochondrion that spans the complete length of the cell.
source: Trypanosomes have a single mitochondrion that spans the complete length of the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome cell biology.

claim: In bloodstream T. brucei, the mitochondrion has a tubular cristae-poor morphology.
source: In BS T. brucei, the mitochondrion has a tubular cristae-poor morphology and the parasites produce ATP by glycolysis and possibly also by substrate-level phosphorylation reactions in the mitochondrial matrix (Zíková et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Procyclic T. brucei have a highly reticulated, cristae-rich mitochondrion and generate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, PC cells have a highly reticulated, cristae-rich mitochondrion and generate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the differences between bloodstream and procyclic forms of T. brucei.

claim: Procyclic T. brucei have a high demand for mitochondrial iron sulfur cluster proteins.
source: PC T. brucei have a high demand for mitochondrial iron sulfur cluster proteins (Lukeš and Basu, 2015), the synthesis of which usually involves GSH (Lill et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Virtually nothing is known about the low-molecular-weight thiols that reside in the mitochondrion of trypanosomatids.
source: However, virtually nothing is known about the low-molecular-weight thiols that reside in the mitochondrion of trypanosomatids (Manta et al., 2013; Tomás and Castro, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: At an equimolar concentration of 1 µM, Tpx-roGFP2 responded slightly faster to Gsp2 and TS2 than to GSSG.
source: At an equimolar concentration of 1 µM, Tpx-roGFP2 responded slightly faster to Gsp2 and TS2 than to GSSG (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: hGrx1-roGFP2 was rapidly oxidized by GSSG.
source: As previously published, hGrx1-roGFP2 was rapidly oxidized by GSSG (Gutscher et al., 2008; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: hGrx1-roGFP2 was efficiently oxidized by Gsp2.
source: The same sensor was also efficiently oxidized by Gsp2 (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: hGrx1-roGFP2 oxidation by TS2 required a 10-times higher concentration than GSSG or Gsp2.
source: whereas a comparable reaction with TS2 required a 10-times higher concentration (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), possibly due to the steric constrains imposed by the cyclic disulfide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Unfused roGFP2 did not react efficiently with any of the disulfides at 1 µM concentration.
source: Unfused roGFP2 did not react efficiently with any of the disulfides (at 1 µM) and at high concentrations was more efficiently oxidized by Gsp2 and TS2 than by GSSG (Figure 1G–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-I.

claim: Fusion to either Tpx or hGrx1 accelerated roGFP2 oxidation by all three disulfides.
source: In conclusion, the fusion to either Tpx or hGrx1 accelerated roGFP2 oxidation by all three disulfides.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing the three sensors.

claim: Tpx-roGFP2 was readily reduced by 100 µM Gsp and 10 µM T(SH)2 whereas 100 µM GSH did not cause any reaction.
source: Tpx-roGFP2 was readily reduced by 100 µM Gsp and 10 µM T(SH)2 whereas 100 µM GSH did not cause any reaction (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Reduction of Tpx-roGFP2 by even 1 mM GSH was very slow.
source: Reduction of Tpx-roGFP2 by even 1 mM GSH was very slow.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: 500 µM T(SH)2 resulted in almost complete Tpx-roGFP2 reduction within five minutes.
source: In contrast, 500 µM T(SH)2 resulted in almost complete probe reduction within five min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: hGrx1-roGFP2 showed virtually the same low reduction rate when treated with 100 µM GSH, 100 µM Gsp or 10 µM T(SH)2.
source: In comparison, hGrx1-roGFP2 showed virtually the same low reduction rate when treated with 100 µM GSH, 100 µM Gsp or 10 µM T(SH)2 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: For significant reduction of hGrx1-roGFP2, ≥500 µM of either GSH or T(SH)2 were required.
source: Clearly, for significant reduction, ≥500 µM of either GSH or T(SH)2 were required (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and F.

claim: The selectivity of hGrx1-roGFP2 for GSH applies to cells with an exclusive glutathione system, but not to Kinetoplastida.
source: This finding indicated that the selectivity of hGrx1-roGFP2 for GSH applies to cells with an exclusive glutathione system, but not to Kinetoplastida.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hGrx1-roGFP2 responds to T(SH)2 in trypanosomes.

claim: Unfused roGFP2 was not reduced by 15 mM GSH, but fully reduced by 7.5 mM T(SH)2.
source: Unfused roGFP2 was not even reduced by 15 mM GSH, but fully reduced by 7.5 mM T(SH)2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and I.

claim: All three sensors were most efficiently reduced by T(SH)2.
source: Taken together, all three sensors were most efficiently reduced by T(SH)2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing reduction of the three sensors by different thiols.

claim: Live cell imaging displayed intense fluorescence equally distributed over the whole cell body in accordance with cytosolic localization of the sensors.
source: Live cell imaging displayed an intense fluorescence that was equally distributed over the whole cell body in accordance with a cytosolic localization (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Under normal culture conditions, all three cytosolic sensors showed an OxD of close to zero indicating they are almost fully reduced in the cytosolic environment.
source: Under normal culture conditions, all three sensors showed an OxD of close to zero indicating that they are almost fully reduced in the cytosolic environment (Figure 3B–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-G.

claim: Exposure of parasites to exogenous H2O2 resulted in concentration-dependent oxidation of the cytosolic probes.
source: Exposure of the parasites to exogenous H2O2 resulted in a concentration-dependent oxidation of the probes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent sensor oxidation.

claim: When 5 µM H2O2 was applied, Tpx-roGFP2 was oxidized within seconds to an OxD of 0.8.
source: When 5 µM H2O2was applied, Tpx-roGFP2 was oxidized within seconds to an OxD of 0.8 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Oxidation of roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2 by 5 µM H2O2 was slightly slower than Tpx-roGFP2 and yielded a maximum OxD of about 0.6 and 0.4, respectively.
source: Oxidation of roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2 was slightly slower and yielded a maximum OxD of about 0.6 and 0.4, respectively (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: Re-reduction after H2O2 treatment was fastest for Tpx-roGFP2.
source: Also, the re-reduction was fastest in the case of Tpx-roGFP2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the three sensors.

claim: Nine minutes after treating cells with 10 µM H2O2, Tpx-roGFP2 was again fully reduced, whereas roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2 required 15 min and 22 min, respectively.
source: Nine min after treating the cells with 10 µM H2O2, the sensor was again fully reduced, whereas roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2 required 15 min and 22 min, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Both Tpx-roGFP2 and roGFP2-hGrx1 showed a stronger response than roGFP2, confirming that detection of transient redox changes by the probes is facilitated by the fused oxidoreductase.
source: Both Tpx-roGFP2 and roGFP2-hGrx1 showed a stronger response than roGFP2, confirming that the detection of transient redox changes by the probes is facilitated by the fused oxidoreductase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the sensor responses.

claim: The response of roGFP2 requires interaction with an endogenous oxidoreductase, most probably Tpx.
source: In contrast, the response of roGFP2 requires the interaction with an endogenous oxidoreductase, most probably Tpx.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that unfused roGFP2 still responds to oxidants, and later confirmed by Tpx depletion experiments.

claim: Both fusion probes respond primarily to changes in the T(SH)2/TS2 redox couple in trypanosomes.
source: Making the assumption that the thiol concentration in the cytosol is comparable to that in the total cell lysate (see Figure 4B), we conclude that both fusion probes respond primarily to changes in the T(SH)2/TS2 redox couple.
evidence: This is inferred from the thiol concentrations measured and the in vitro reactivity data.

claim: Tpx-roGFP2 sensor is insensitive towards micromolar H2O2 concentrations.
source: The data demonstrated that also the Tpx-roGFP2 sensor is insensitive towards micromolar H2O2 concentrations and confirmed previous studies on hGrx1-roGFP2 and roGFP2 (Gutscher et al., 2008; Kasozi et al., 2013; Müller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no direct oxidation by H2O2 and citations to previous studies.

claim: All three cytosolic sensors completely recovered when cells were treated with up to 20 µM H2O2.
source: All three sensors completely recovered when cells were treated with up to 20 µM H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: A second H2O2 bolus elicited an almost identical response, demonstrating full reversibility of the sensor response.
source: A second H2O2 bolus elicited an almost identical response, demonstrating full reversibility of the response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: After exposing cells to 50 µM H2O2, the sensors remained partially oxidized, and a second H2O2 bolus did not trigger any further oxidation.
source: In contrast, after exposing the cells to 50 µM H2O2, the sensors remained partially oxidized, and a second H2O2 bolus did not trigger any further oxidation (Figure 3B, D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, D and F.

claim: When diamide was used as a second bolus treatment after 50 µM H2O2, all sensors were again oxidized, ruling out irreversible probe inactivation by hyperoxidation.
source: However, when diamide was used as a second bolus treatment, all sensors were again oxidized, ruling out irreversible probe inactivation by hyperoxidation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The cPrx was likely hyperoxidized and inactivated by high H2O2 concentration, abrogating the Prx-catalyzed generation of TS2 responsible for oxidizing the roGFP2-based probes.
source: Most likely, the cPrx was hyperoxidized and inactivated by the high H2O2 concentration, thus abrogating the Prx-catalyzed generation of TS2 responsible for oxidizing the roGFP2-based probes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that sensors don't respond to a second H2O2 pulse after 50 µM treatment.

claim: When cells were challenged with diamide, Tpx-roGFP2 was rapidly oxidized but to a lower maximum OxD than cells expressing roGFP2-hGrx1 or roGFP2.
source: When the cells were challenged with a single bolus of 10 µM or 30 µM diamide, Tpx-roGFP2 was rapidly oxidized, but to a lower maximum OxD than cells expressing roGFP2-hGrx1 or roGFP2 (Figure 3C,E G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, E, G.

claim: All sensors became fully oxidized upon exposure of cells to 100 µM diamide, suggesting they were directly oxidized.
source: All sensors became fully oxidized upon exposure of the cells to 100 µM diamide, suggesting that they were directly oxidized.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all sensors reach full oxidation at high diamide concentration.

claim: Probe recovery from diamide stress was slower than from H2O2 stress.
source: In general, probe recovery (from comparable OxD maxima) was slower in diamide- than in H2O2-treated cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing recovery times.

claim: Diamide treatment of PC cells may primarily lead to formation of protein mixed disulfides which are more slowly reduced than TS2.
source: As observed in BS T. brucei (Ulrich et al., 2017), diamide treatment of the PC cells may primarily lead to the formation of protein mixed disulfides which, most likely, are more slowly reduced than TS2.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations in BS T. brucei and supported by a citation.

claim: After both H2O2- and diamide-stress, re-reduction of Tpx-roGFP2 was fastest, followed by roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2, corroborating the kinetic superiority of the Tpx-coupled sensor.
source: After both H2O2- and diamide-stress, re-reduction of Tpx-roGFP2 was fastest, followed by roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2, corroborating the kinetic superiority of the Tpx-coupled sensor also under in vivo conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing sensor recovery rates under different stress conditions.

claim: After 48 hr of DFMO treatment, cells displayed a significant proliferation defect.
source: After 48 hr, DFMO-treated cells displayed a significant proliferation defect (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Growth of DFMO-treated cells almost stopped after 72 hr.
source: and growth almost stopped after 72 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: No difference was observed between WT parasites and cells expressing Tpx-roGFP2 in response to DFMO, ruling out any effect of the sensor on the parasites' sensitivity towards DFMO.
source: No difference was observed between WT parasites and cells expressing Tpx-roGFP2, ruling out any effect of the sensor on the parasites' sensitivity towards DFMO.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing WT and sensor-expressing cells.

claim: In untreated WT cells, total GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations were 134 ± 8 µM and 521 ± 34 µM, respectively.
source: When untreated WT cells were lysed in the presence of TCEP, we obtained total GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations of 134 ± 8 µM and 521 ± 34 µM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In cells cultured for 48 hr in the presence of DFMO, GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations were 322 ± 24 µM and 210 ± 17 µM, respectively.
source: In cells cultured for 48 hr in the presence of DFMO, the GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations were 322 ± 24 µM and 210 ± 17 µM, respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In DFMO treated cells, the GSH concentration was doubled, whereas the T(SH)2 concentration was halved.
source: Thus, in DFMO treated cells, the GSH concentration was doubled, whereas the T(SH)2 concentration was halved, in agreement with published data (Bellofatto et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the measurements, supported by a citation to published data.

claim: When parasites were disintegrated in the absence of TCEP, thiol values were 10–20% lower, indicating that cellular thiols are mainly in the reduced state.
source: When the parasites were disintegrated in the absence of the reducing agent TCEP, the values in all samples were 10–20% lower, indicating that the cellular thiols are mainly in the reduced state as previously shown for BS T. brucei (Ulrich et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous work.

claim: DFMO treatment did not cause any shift of intracellular thiol/disulfide ratios.
source: Clearly, DFMO treatment did not cause any shift of intracellular thiol/disulfide ratios.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most thiols remain reduced even after DFMO treatment.

claim: The basal OxD of Tpx-roGFP2 sensor was almost zero, independently if cells had been cultured in the absence or presence of DFMO.
source: The basal OxD of the Tpx-roGFP2 sensor was almost zero, independently if the cells had been cultured in the absence or presence of DFMO (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The altered GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations in DFMO-treated cells had no effect on the steady state thiol/disulfide ratios in the cytosol.
source: indicating that the altered GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations had no effect on the steady state thiol/disulfide ratios in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged basal OxD of the sensor.

claim: The rate and degree of sensor oxidation triggered by exogenously applied H2O2 was unaffected by DFMO treatment.
source: The rate and degree of sensor oxidation triggered by exogenously applied H2O2 was also unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Recovery of reduced Tpx-roGFP2 appeared to be slightly delayed in cells that had been cultured in the presence of DFMO after H2O2 treatment.
source: However, recovery of reduced Tpx-roGFP2 appeared to be slightly delayed in cells that had been cultured in the presence of DFMO (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon diamide stress, reductive recovery was clearly delayed in DFMO-treated cells.
source: Upon diamide stress, reductive recovery was clearly delayed in the drug-treated cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Parasites with diminished cellular T(SH)2 content exhibit decreased reductive capacity when exposed to an oxidative insult.
source: In summary, parasites with diminished cellular T(SH)2 content exhibit decreased reductive capacity when exposed to an oxidative insult.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DFMO experiments showing delayed recovery.

claim: After 24 hr of RNAi, Tpx was significantly down-regulated.
source: After 24 hr of RNAi, Tpx was significantly down-regulated (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: After 24 hr of Tpx RNAi, proliferation was not yet affected.
source: but proliferation was not yet affected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: After 72 hr of Tpx RNAi, the cells died in accordance with the fact that Tpx is essential.
source: After 72 hr the cells died in accordance with the fact that Tpx is essential (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and established knowledge that Tpx is essential.

claim: The same behavior was previously observed for BS T. brucei, and attributed to a transient increase in the free thiol levels.
source: The same behavior was previously observed for BS T. brucei, and attributed to a transient increase in the free thiol levels (Comini et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: For Tpx-depleted PC cells, GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations were 10–20% higher compared to non-induced controls.
source: For Tpx-depleted PC cells, we obtained 10–20% higher GSH and T(SH)2 concentrations compared to the non-induced controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The sensor response towards exogenous H2O2 in non-induced Tpx RNAi cells was identical to that in the parental cell line.
source: As expected, the sensor response towards exogenous H2O2 in non-induced cells was identical to that in the parental cell line (Figure 5C and D, left graphs and Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D (left graphs) and Figure 3D and F.

claim: In Tpx-induced cells, the sensors still showed a basal OxD of almost zero indicating that Tpx depletion did not affect the cytosolic T(SH)2/TS2 steady state ratio.
source: In the induced cells, the sensors still showed a basal OxD of almost zero indicating that Tpx depletion as such did not affect the cytosolic T(SH)2/TS2 steady state ratio.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Both roGFP2-hGrx1 and roGFP2 reacted only marginally when Tpx-depleted cells were challenged with H2O2.
source: However, both sensors reacted only marginally when the cells were challenged with H2O2 (Figure 5C and D, right graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D (right graphs).

claim: In the absence of Tpx, the parasite peroxidases are unable to reduce H2O2.
source: In the absence of Tpx, the parasite peroxidases are unable to reduce H2O2.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of sensor response in Tpx-depleted cells.

claim: The spontaneous formation of TS2 in the direct reaction of H2O2 with T(SH)2 is probably too slow to result in measurable probe oxidation.
source: Under these conditions, H2O2 can only be reduced by a direct reaction with T(SH)2 (Hillebrand et al., 2003). The spontaneous formation of TS2 in this reaction is probably too slow (and the subsequent reduction of TS2 by TR too fast) to result in measurable probe oxidation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that sensors don't respond in Tpx-depleted cells, supported by a citation.

claim: PC parasites lacking Px I-III undergo a ferroptosis-like cell death that starts at the mitochondrion.
source: PC parasites lacking Px I-III undergo a ferroptosis-like cell death that starts at the mitochondrion.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claim: Px-depleted cells are fully viable and proliferative if the medium is supplemented with Trolox.
source: The cells are, however, fully viable and proliferative if the medium is supplemented with Trolox (Bogacz and Krauth-Siegel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: 1.5 hr after Trolox withdrawal, all three Px-depleted cell lines still displayed a basal OxD of zero and responded to H2O2 like the parental cell line, yet sensor reduction was slightly delayed.
source: 1.5 hr after Trolox withdrawal, all three cell lines still displayed a basal OxD of zero and responded to a bolus of H2O2 like the parental cell line, yet sensor reduction was slightly delayed (Figure 6, left graphs and Figure 3B,D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 (left graphs) and Figure 3B, D and F.

claim: After 3 hr in the absence of Trolox, the basal OxD of all three sensors in Px-depleted cells increased during the course of the experiment.
source: After 3 hr in the absence of Trolox, the basal OxD of all three sensors increased during the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 (central graphs).

claim: The response to exogenous H2O2 was weaker and sensors were only partially re-reduced when Px-depleted cells were treated with 20 µM H2O2 after 3 hr without Trolox.
source: The response to an exogenous H2O2 bolus was weaker and the sensors were only partially re-reduced when cells were treated with 20 µM H2O2 (Figure 6, central graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 (central graphs).

claim: After keeping Px-depleted cells without Trolox for 4 or 4.5 hr, the sensors reported a basal OxD of 0.1–0.3 which further increased to 0.4–0.6 towards the end of the measurement.
source: After keeping cells without Trolox for 4 or 4.5 hr, the sensors reported a basal OxD of 0.1–0.3 which further increased to 0.4–0.6 towards the end of the measurement (Figure 6, right graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 (right graphs).

claim: In the absence of Trolox, the cytosolic probes in Px-depleted cells were increasingly oxidized over time.
source: Taken together, in the absence of Trolox, the cytosolic probes were increasingly oxidized over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course data in Px-depleted cells.

claim: Cells unable to reduce lipid hydroperoxides suffer a decrease in the cytosolic T(SH)2/TS2 ratio, associated with an impaired ability to cope with exogenously applied oxidants.
source: These findings demonstrate that cells that are unable to reduce lipid hydroperoxides suffer a decrease in the cytosolic T(SH)2/TS2 ratio, associated with an impaired ability to cope with exogenously applied oxidants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Px depletion experiments.

claim: Oxidation of the cytosolic trypanothione pool precedes lysis of Px-depleted cells.
source: Oxidation of the cytosolic trypanothione pool precedes lysis of Px-depleted cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sensor oxidation occurs before cell death.

claim: Live cell fluorescence microscopy confirmed the specific localization of the mitochondrial sensors in the single mitochondrion of the parasite.
source: Live cell fluorescence microscopy confirmed the specific localization of the probes in the single mitochondrion of the parasite (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The matrix-targeted mito-roGFP2-Tpx, mito-roGFP2-hGrx1, and mito-roGFP2 reported a steady state OxD of about 0.1.
source: The matrix-targeted mito-roGFP2-Tpx, mito-roGFP2-hGrx1, and mito-roGFP2 reported a steady state OxD of about 0.1 (Figure 7B–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-G.

claim: When parasites were exposed to exogenous oxidants, all three mitochondrial probes were oxidized to a higher degree and were more slowly re-reduced than the respective cytosolic sensors.
source: When the parasites were exposed to exogenous oxidants, all three mitochondrial probes were oxidized to a higher degree and were more slowly re-reduced than the respective cytosolic sensors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mitochondrial and cytosolic sensor responses.

claim: The reducing capacity in the single mitochondrion of trypanosomes is comparably low which could be due to a diminished T(SH)2/TS2 ratio and/or low total thiol concentration.
source: This indicates that the reducing capacity in the single mitochondrion of trypanosomes is comparably low which could be due to a diminished T(SH)2/TS2 ratio and/or low total thiol concentration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of slower recovery and higher oxidation of mitochondrial sensors.

claim: In contrast to the cytosolic sensors, the mitochondrial probes responded to a second pulse of 50 µM H2O2.
source: In contrast to the cytosolic sensors, the mitochondrial probes responded to a second pulse of 50 µM H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The mPrx is less prone to over-oxidation than the cPrx or less H2O2 reaches the mitochondrion due to the buffering capacity of the cytosol.
source: This suggested that the mPrx is less prone to over-oxidation than the cPrx as shown for mammalian Prx3 (Cox et al., 2010); or less H2O2 reaches the mitochondrion due to the buffering capacity of the cytosol (Calabrese et al., 2019; Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that mitochondrial sensors respond to a second H2O2 pulse, supported by citations.

claim: The de novo synthesis of T(SH)2 and the reduction of TS2 are confined to the cytosol.
source: The de novo synthesis of T(SH)2 and the reduction of TS2 are confined to the cytosol (Oza et al., 2005; Smith et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Specific transporters for T(SH)2/TS2 have not been identified.
source: So far, specific transporters for T(SH)2/TS2 have not been identified.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: In yeast and human cells, the biosynthesis of GSH is cytosolic, but GR occurs in both the cytosol and mitochondrial matrix.
source: In yeast and human cells, the biosynthesis of GSH is also cytosolic, but GR occurs in both the cytosol and mitochondrial matrix (Calabrese et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In rabbit kidney mitochondria and mitoplasts, the dicarboxylate carrier (DIC) and oxoglutarate carrier (OGC) were identified as GSH transporters in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: In rabbit kidney mitochondria and mitoplasts, the dicarboxylate carrier (DIC) and oxoglutarate carrier (OGC) were identified as GSH transporters in the inner mitochondrial membrane (Chen et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Transport of GSH in Lactococcus lactis is independent of the two anion carriers.
source: whereas transport of GSH in Lactococcus lactis is independent of the two anion carriers (Booty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In T. brucei, the mitochondrial carrier protein 12 (MCP12) acts as carboxylate and tricarboxylate carrier, fulfilling the functions of DIC and OGC.
source: In T. brucei, the mitochondrial carrier protein 12 (MCP12) was shown to act as carboxylate and tricarboxylate carrier, thereby fulfilling the functions of DIC and OGC (Colasante et al., 2009; Colasante et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Due to its overall positive charge, it is highly unlikely that T(SH)2 is imported by MCP12.
source: Due to its overall positive charge, it is highly unlikely that T(SH)2 is imported by these transporters.
evidence: This is speculation based on the chemical properties of T(SH)2 and the known function of MCP12.

claim: Regeneration of reduced mitochondrial hGrx1-roGFP2 in oxidatively challenged yeast cells requires the matrix-localized GR.
source: Regeneration of reduced mitochondrial hGrx1-roGFP2 in oxidatively challenged yeast cells requires the matrix-localized GR (Kojer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Trypanosomes may possess a protein that mediates an exchange of TS2 and T(SH)2 over the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: One may thus speculate that trypanosomes possess a protein that mediates an exchange of TS2 and T(SH)2 over the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that mitochondrial sensors respond to trypanothione redox changes despite cytosolic biosynthesis.

claim: Unfused mito-roGFP2 responded to exogenous H2O2, pointing to the presence of an oxidoreductase that facilitates equilibration of the sensor with the mitochondrial T(SH)2/TS2 couple.
source: The finding that unfused mito-roGFP2 responded to exogenous H2O2 pointed to the presence of an oxidoreductase that facilitates the equilibration of the sensor with the mitochondrial T(SH)2/TS2 couple and is capable of transferring reducing equivalents from T(SH)2 onto the mitochondrial peroxidases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unfused mito-roGFP2 responds to H2O2.

claim: Re-reduction of mito-roGFP2 was slow compared to cytosolic roGFP2.
source: Nevertheless, re-reduction of mito-roGFP2 was slow when compared to cytosolic roGFP2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the two sensors.

claim: The catalytic capacity of the mitochondrial oxidoreductase appears to be limited due to either low reactivity or low concentration.
source: The catalytic capacity of the mitochondrial oxidoreductase appears to be limited due to either low reactivity or low concentration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the slow re-reduction of mito-roGFP2.

claim: Tpx-depletion affected the response of mito-roGFP2 and mito-roGFP2-hGrx1.
source: Tpx-depletion affected the response of mito-roGFP2 and mito-roGFP2-hGrx1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: A minor fraction of Tpx may reside in the mitochondrion.
source: One putative explanation may be that a minor fraction of Tpx resides in the mitochondrion. This would be in agreement with immuno-electron microscopy data which revealed some gold particles in the mitochondrion (Tetaud et al., 2001)
evidence: This is speculation based on the partial effect of Tpx depletion on mitochondrial sensors, supported by a citation to immuno-EM data.

claim: Tpx-depletion did not fully abolish the response of the mitochondrial sensors to exogenous H2O2.
source: Notably, Tpx-depletion did not fully abolish the response of the mitochondrial sensors to exogenous H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Another oxidoreductase can mediate the electron transfer between T(SH)2 and the mitochondrial peroxidases.
source: Probably, another oxidoreductase can mediate the electron transfer between T(SH)2 and the mitochondrial peroxidases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mitochondrial sensors still respond to H2O2 after Tpx depletion.

claim: Depletion of mPrx in PC T. brucei over three days results in undetectable levels of the protein.
source: Depletion of mPrx in PC T. brucei over three days results in undetectable levels of the protein.
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data.

claim: At three days of mPrx depletion, cells still proliferate like WT cells.
source: At this time point, the cells still proliferate like WT cells
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data.

claim: After seven days of mPrx depletion, proliferation is severely affected and parasites display a highly elongated shape.
source: whereas after seven days of depletion, proliferation is severely affected and the parasites display a highly elongated shape (Bogacz et al. unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data.

claim: The altered morphology of mPrx-depleted cells had no effect on the expression level and subcellular targeting of the sensors.
source: The altered morphology of the mPrx-depleted cells had no effect on the expression level and subcellular targeting of the sensors (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Non-induced mPrx RNAi cells displayed the same sensor response as the respective parental strain.
source: Non-induced cells displayed the same sensor response as the respective parental strain (Figure 9B–E, left graphs compare with Figure 7B,D and F and Figure 3B,D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B-E (left graphs) compared to Figure 7 and Figure 3.

claim: In mPrx-depleted cells, the basal OxD of all sensors was unchanged.
source: In mPrx-depleted cells, the basal OxD of all sensors was unchanged (Figure 9B–E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B-E.

claim: The basal OxD being unchanged in mPrx-depleted cells indicates that neither the mitochondrial nor the cytosolic T(SH)2/TS2 ratio was affected.
source: indicating that neither the mitochondrial nor the cytosolic T(SH)2/TS2 ratio was affected.
evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged basal OxD.

claim: Depletion of mPrx had a strong impact on the sensor response when cells were exposed to exogenous H2O2.
source: However, depletion of mPrx had a strong impact on the sensor response when the cells were exposed to exogenous H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: In cells subjected to mPrx RNAi for three days, the mitochondrial sensors showed virtually no oxidation when 5 µM or 10 µM H2O2 was applied.
source: In cells subjected to RNAi for three days, the mitochondrial sensors showed virtually no oxidation when 5 µM or 10 µM H2O2 was applied.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and C (middle graphs).

claim: Addition of 20 µM H2O2 to cells with three days of mPrx depletion resulted in a slow and minor increase in OxD, together with delayed reductive recovery.
source: Addition of 20 µM H2O2 resulted in a slow and minor increase in OxD, together with a delayed reductive recovery (Figure 9B and C, middle graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and C (middle graphs).

claim: After seven days of mPrx depletion, oxidation of the mitochondrial sensors was again increased and re-reduction even more delayed.
source: After seven days of mPrx depletion, oxidation of the mitochondrial sensors was again increased and re-reduction even more delayed (Figure 9B and C, right graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and C (right graphs).

claim: RNAi against mPrx had a strong effect on the response of the cytosolic sensors.
source: Interestingly, RNAi against mPrx had also a strong effect on the response of the cytosolic sensors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: In cells subjected to mPrx depletion for three days and exposed to 20 µM H2O2, re-reduction of cytosolic Tpx-roGFP2 was slowed down and roGFP2 showed a slightly increased OxD peak.
source: In cells subjected to mPrx depletion for three days and exposed to a bolus of 20 µM H2O2, re-reduction of cytosolic Tpx-roGFP2 was slowed down and roGFP2 showed a slightly increased OxD peak (Figure 9D and E, middle graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D and E (middle graphs).

claim: In cells induced for seven days of mPrx depletion and treated with 20 µM H2O2, Tpx-roGFP2 displayed an OxD peak lasting for at least 10 min.
source: In cells induced for seven days and treated with 20 µM H2O2, Tpx-roGFP2 displayed an OxD peak lasting for at least 10 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D (right graph).

claim: At all H2O2 concentrations used, re-reduction of cytosolic Tpx-roGFP2 was markedly attenuated in cells with seven days of mPrx depletion relative to non-induced cells.
source: At all H2O2 concentrations used, re-reduction of cytosolic Tpx-roGFP2 was markedly attenuated relative to non-induced cells (Figure 9D, right and left graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D (right and left graphs).

claim: After seven days of mPrx depletion, roGFP2 was oxidized to a higher degree and for a longer time.
source: At this time point, also roGFP2 was oxidized to a higher degree and for a longer time (Figure 9E, right graph).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E (right graph).

claim: Depletion of mPrx affected the response of mito-roGFP2-Tpx and mito-roGFP2 to a challenge with exogenous H2O2.
source: Thus, depletion of mPrx affected the response of mito-roGFP2-Tpx and mito-roGFP2 to a challenge with exogenous H2O2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: mPrx is involved in the reduction of exogenously applied H2O2 and is the main mitochondrial H2O2-metabolising thiol peroxidase.
source: This indicates that mPrx is involved in the reduction of exogenously applied H2O2 and is the main mitochondrial H2O2-metabolising thiol peroxidase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mPrx depletion strongly reduces mitochondrial sensor response to H2O2.

claim: H2O2 can still be reduced by Px III in mPrx-depleted cells.
source: However, the mitochondrial sensor response was not completely lost. Probably, H2O2 can still be reduced by Px III (Bogacz and Krauth-Siegel, 2018; Diechtierow and Krauth-Siegel, 2011; Schaffroth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that mitochondrial sensors still respond partially after mPrx depletion, supported by citations.

claim: In cells subjected to long-term mPrx depletion, reduction of exogenously applied H2O2 in the cytosol was strongly delayed.
source: In cells that were subjected to long-term mPrx depletion, reduction of exogenously applied H2O2 in the cytosol was strongly delayed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The delayed cytosolic H2O2 reduction in long-term mPrx-depleted cells may be due to a general impairment of metabolism in these proliferation arrested cells.
source: One may speculate that this is due to a general impairment of metabolism in these proliferation arrested cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that long-term mPrx-depleted cells are growth-arrested.

claim: The high selectivity of roGFP2-hGrx1 for the GSH/GSSG redox couple is restricted to cells that do not convert GSH into additional closely related low molecular weight thiols such as Gsp and T(SH)2.
source: Notably, our data also reveal that the high selectivity of roGFP2-hGrx1 for the GSH/GSSG redox couple is restricted to cells that do not convert GSH into additional closely related low molecular weight thiols such as Gsp and T(SH)2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that roGFP2-hGrx1 responds to T(SH)2 in trypanosomes.

claim: In trypanosomes, roGFP2-hGrx1 predominantly equilibrates with the T(SH)2/TS2 redox couple.
source: In trypanosomes, roGFP2-hGrx1 predominantly equilibrates with the T(SH)2/TS2 redox couple.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study, supported by in vitro and in vivo data.
